message:
fix: stop copying the material into tray_sub_brands for a 3rd party slot

The dashboard builds the readable name from vendor, material and filament
name, and a chipless slot has only the material the user set on the AMS.
Copying it into tray_sub_brands so the name field had something to show
put it in twice, as "PLA . PLA". The projection drops the "N/A"
placeholder on its own now, so the copy has nothing left to do.

It also wrote into the record that is kept as printer.lastAmsData, which
is the baseline the next report is compared against, so the comparison
ran against a value the printer never sent.

Verified against the live printer in a container: A0 empty and A1 holding
a chipless PLA spool now read "Empty slot" and "PLA".

author: (a person)
message:
fix(llvm): target the host CPU in the JIT on LLVM 9

On LLVM 9, JITTargetMachineBuilder::detectHost sets only the target
triple. LLVM 10 changed it to also set the host CPU name and features.
The LLVM 9 JIT therefore generated code for generic x86-64, while the
compiler checked the host features and emitted SSE4.1 intrinsics. The
JIT then failed in instruction selection with "Cannot select
X86ISD::VRNDSCALE" on f32.nearest and f32x4.nearest. On LLVM 9, give
the LLJIT builder a target machine builder with the host CPU name and
features, as LLVM 10 does.

author: (a person)
message:
fix(core): define embedding readiness by what retrieval uses

Review on #1440 found the embedding counts wrong in both directions, which is
one bug with two signs: neither side of the comparison was defined by what
semantic retrieval actually does.

- Settled when it was not: `embedded` accepted any `ready` manifest row, so a
  chunk left behind by an embedding-model or vector-index change still counted.
  With every entity in that state readiness reported IDLE and `status --wait`
  returned before embeddings were usable.
- Pending when it was not: `embeddable` counted every Markdown entity, including
  ones whose note sets `embed: false`. `sync_entity_vectors_batch` deliberately
  clears and skips those, so `embedded` could never reach `embeddable` and the
  stage stayed PENDING forever.

Both sides now come from the definition that owns them. The manifest conditions
vector hydration admits are lifted into one shared constant,
`CURRENT_VECTOR_MANIFEST_PREDICATE`, applied by both hydration and readiness so
a change to retrieval has a single place to keep in step. The owed side applies
`entity_embeddings_enabled`, the same opt-out policy sync uses. The comparison
is a set difference rather than a subtraction, which drops the `max(0, ...)`
clamp: an entity can hold a usable vector and no longer be owed one.

One part is deliberately not covered, and says so in the code: that a ready
manifest row still has its physical vector. The only portable check needs a
search repository, and constructing one loads the embedding model — a cost a
polled status route must not pay, and one that also deadlocked a size-1 test
pool through nested session acquisition. `bm project info` verifies it through
`ProjectService.get_embedding_status` and recommends a rebuild.

Separately, `bm project add` reported a post-creation failure as a failure to
create. The project row is durable before indexing starts, so "Error adding
project" both misnamed the failure and sent the user back to a command that now
refuses with "already exists". Creation and the follow-up work are now separate
try blocks with separate outcomes; the second names the step that failed and
prints the remedy that works from here. That block also covers the other
post-persist steps the old handler hid — the cloud config save and the local
sync-path mkdir.

message:
test(api): self-seed unique users in user.test.ts and drop partial-email [0] dependency

The shared fixed email '(a person)' was reused across three tests with no
cleanup, and findUsersByPartOfEmail relied on the [0] of an unordered result.
Under parallel jest workers sharing the test DB, a stale same-email user (or a
sibling block's seed user) could shift that [0], making the assertion order-
dependent and contributing to cross-block state bleed.

Create one unique-email user (aoi-<base36 ts>@example.com) once in a describe
beforeAll and tear it down with User.deleteOne in afterAll. Select the target
user by its known email (find(u => u.email === email)) instead of [0], and fold
the standalone 'should created' case into the beforeAll seed. Test-only; no
production code touched.

author: (a person)
message:
Close the code review 33 findings on the Data Manager lanes

Seven findings from the first review of phases 3 and 4, none above Low,
fixed together because five of them are one-line guards and the other two
are the design decisions the review asked for.

The one that did nothing: uninstall asked Action Scheduler to cancel the
plugin's queued sends by hook, group and an empty argument list, and with a
group given the library reads an empty argument list as "actions scheduled
with no arguments", which none of ours are. Nothing was ever cancelled on
that backend (the WP-Cron half worked), and the tests stayed green because
both stubs recorded the hook and the group and ignored the arguments. The
call now names the hook alone, which is the library's bulk cancel-by-hook
path, the stubs record every parameter, and the dead SendQueue method that
duplicated the loop is gone - uninstall owns it, since it cannot autoload.

The two decisions. A consent denial recorded with an order now keeps the
identifiers it forbids out of that order whatever the confirmation page
posts later: the backfill route applied the consent gate to the posted map
only, so a buyer who refused analytics at checkout and agreed on the receipt
page ended up with identifiers stored beside a record that said no. The
record itself is untouched, as before; it is what the send lane reads. And
the confirmation page reached through Easy Digital Downloads' own receipt
links, which carry the order id and a verification hash rather than the
payment key, now hands the route that hash instead of printing the key the
address bar never held; the route accepts either proof through the one
receipt-hash rule the confirmation page already applied.

The guards: the WooCommerce refund adapter refuses a refund whose parent is
not the order it was paired with, as the EDD adapter already did (nothing on
a request path can produce such a pair; this protects the stored
references); the gtm4wp_gdm_order_consent filter receives the resolved order
on the backfill path - the WC_Order object, the EDD order id - instead of the
request's raw string, so a callback written against order creation no longer
fatals on the one path the plugin's own script posts to; and the status poll
cleans the result it writes into the send log through the same helper every
other text member takes.

Every behavioural change ships a test that was red on the previous source;
the two refusal tests for the hash proof are must-not-break guards and green
by design.

author: (a person)
message:
Use UplinkState for CUDN gateways

Build CUDN L3 gateway configuration from UplinkState when a
primary L2 or L3 CUDN references an Uplink.

Translate resolved host gateway MACs, addresses, default gateways,
and OVS bridge names into the existing L3GatewayConfig shape used by
GatewayManager.

Filter imported BGP routes for Uplink-backed CUDNs to the Linux link
index of the resolved Uplink bridge. This prevents default-VRF route
leaks from programming GR nexthops that are reachable only through
another bridge.

Add a shared level-driven controller for Uplink-backed CUDNs. The
controller does not own UplinkState; ovnkube-node publishes that
state. Instead, it watches UplinkState, NAD, and network activity
changes and asks the node reconciler to re-run the matching
node/network gateway reconciliation. UplinkState changes also re-run
route import so stale imported GR routes are removed when the
resolved Uplink bridge changes or becomes unavailable.

author: (a person)
message:
Switch devcontainer to docker-in-docker for wp-env bind mounts

docker-outside-of-docker shares the host Docker socket, so bind mount
paths are resolved on the host — not inside the devcontainer. This
prevents wp-env from mounting the plugin directory into its WordPress
container, causing 'plugin could not be found' on activation.

docker-in-docker runs its own Docker daemon inside the devcontainer
where /workspaces/wp-document-revisions is a real path, so wp-env
bind mounts work correctly.
